title: Absence of critical scaling in the Schelling segregation model
abstract: We find no evidence of critical scaling in the Schelling segregation model, in either the Moore neighborhood or its dense-spectrum extension to Chebyshev radii up to $r_0 = 6$ ($k = 168$ neighbors). On periodic grids up to $L = 320$ with 50 trials per point (> 12,500 runs), every finite-size scaling diagnostic in the Moore baseline fails: the per-$L$ $T_c$ does not drift, Var$(S) \sim L^{-2.02 \pm 0.09}$ matches trivial averaging, $γ/ν\approx 0$, and the scaling collapse never reaches a finite optimum. The 8-site Moore neighborhood restricts satisfaction to ratios $j/k$ with $k \leq 8$, giving $S(T)$ a staircase structure with 23 rational thresholds; discreteness alone does not forbid criticality (cf. the Ising model), but the scaling evidence rules it out empirically. A branching-ratio calculation predicts subcritical cascades of mean size $1/(1-R)$ and is validated by perturbation experiments to within 15%; the multiscalar dissimilarity length stays finite across the transition. The dense-spectrum extension strengthens the negative verdict: across $r_0 \in {3,4,5,6}$ on $L \in {40,80,160}$ the Binder cumulant has no $L$-curve crossing and the per-$L$ $T_c$ drift is monotonic and unsaturated; at $r_0 = 4$, extending to $L = 320$ gives $α= -2.70$, below the critical boundary $α= -2$, dissolving an apparent $α= +0.81$ signal visible only on $L \in {40,80}$. The mechanism is the absence of long-range correlation in equilibrium plus deterministic high-$k$ dynamics, not the staircase structure. With a Beta-distributed heterogeneous tolerance, the intolerant tail drives segregation even at moderate population-average tolerance. The staircase theorem and cascade mechanism together account for the Schelling transition without invoking critical phenomena.
summary: This work investigates whether the segregation transition in the Schelling model belongs to a critical universality class. By applying extensive finite-size scaling analysis and examining various dynamic regimes, the authors conclude that the system does not exhibit critical behavior. Instead, the transition is governed by deterministic dynamics related to local satisfaction thresholds.
main_problem: To determine whether the mixed-to-segregated transition in the Schelling segregation model exhibits critical scaling behavior characteristic of a continuous phase transition.
main_result: The analysis strongly rules out criticality, showing that standard finite-size scaling diagnostics fail across multiple neighborhood definitions and lattice sizes. The mechanism is attributed to deterministic dynamics and lack of long-range correlation rather than critical phenomena.
method: The study employs extensive numerical simulations on lattices, utilizing Finite-Size Scaling (FSS) diagnostics like variance analysis and Binder cumulants, alongside mean-field theory and cascade branching ratio calculations.
model_or_system: The Schelling segregation model is simulated on an L x L lattice with periodic boundary conditions. Agents of two types attempt to move when local satisfaction falls below a global tolerance threshold T, leading to segregation.
key_observables: Segregation index (S), interface density (I), variance of S ($	ext{Var}(S)$), Binder cumulant ($U_4$), and the characteristic length scale $r^*$ for dissimilarity.
important_parameters: Lattice size L (up to 320), agent fraction $ho=0.9$, neighborhood radius $r_0$ (up to 6), and tolerance threshold T.
main_assumptions: The analysis compares empirical results against theoretical predictions for critical phenomena, and some parts rely on mean-field approximations or cascade theory assumptions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of segregation index on tolerance, phase diagrams in (T, $ho$), and how $T_c$ shifts when agent tolerances are drawn from a Beta distribution parameterized by $\kappa$.
paper_structure: The paper systematically tests for criticality using FSS diagnostics across various lattice sizes and neighborhood definitions. It contrasts these results with mean-field predictions derived from the satisfaction spectrum, ultimately concluding that non-critical mechanisms govern the transition.
why_interesting: While not quantum mechanical, the rigorous application of critical scaling theory to a classical interacting particle system provides valuable insights into when complex pattern formation transitions are governed by true phase transitions versus deterministic/mean-field crossovers.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Segregation index S and interface density versus tolerance T for L = 80, averaged over 50 trials with per-agent noise σ = 0.02. Shaded regions show ±1 standard deviation.
Figure 2: Equilibrium configurations on an L = 80 grid for selected tolerance values.
Figure 3: Phase diagram in the (T, ρ) plane. Color encodes the equilibrium segregation index. The mixed-segregated boundary is sharp across all densities.

Figure 4: Left: Segregation index vs. tolerance for five system sizes. The curves steepen with L but share the same midpoint. Right: Variance of S at Tc versus system size, with a power-law fit Var(S) ∼L−α, α = 2.02 ± 0.09.
Figure 5: Left: Susceptibility χ(T) for five system sizes. Right: Peak susceptibility vs. L. The scaling exponent γ/ν = −0.015 ± 0.086 is indistinguishable from zero.
